title: Concept Drills — Refraction at Plane Surfaces (Class 11 Physics)
subject: physics

questions.question: A stick in water looks bent at the surface. Explain with the speed change at the boundary.
questions.solution: Light slows in water (v = c/n); the wavefront pivots like a marching column stepping onto slower ground, bending toward the normal. Rays from the submerged part reach the eye along a straight line from an APPARENT position above the true one — hence the bend. Refraction is the wavefront's response to a speed change.

questions.question: When light passes from air into glass, which of speed, frequency and wavelength change and which stay fixed?
questions.solution: Frequency stays fixed — it is set by the SOURCE and cannot change at a boundary (wavefronts cannot pile up or vanish). Speed drops to c/n and wavelength shrinks to λ/n to keep v = fλ consistent. Frequency constant, speed and wavelength change together.

questions.question: A pool 2 m deep appears about 1.5 m deep. Derive the apparent-depth relation and state when it fails.
questions.solution: Rays from the bottom refract AWAY from the normal leaving water, appearing to come from a shallower point. For small angles: apparent depth = real depth/n (2/1.33 ≈ 1.5 m). It fails for large viewing angles — the small-angle approximation (sinθ ≈ tanθ) breaks down and the apparent position shifts with viewing angle.

questions.question: Define critical angle and explain why it exists only when light goes from denser to rarer medium.
questions.solution: The critical angle is the incidence angle in the denser medium for which the refracted ray grazes along the boundary (refraction angle = 90°): sin θc = n_rare/n_denser. Going the other way (rarer → denser), light bends toward the normal and refraction is always possible — no angle produces 90°, so no critical angle exists.

questions.question: State the two conditions for total internal reflection and give one natural and one technological example.
questions.solution: Conditions: (1) light travels from denser to rarer medium; (2) angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. Natural: mirage (light grazing hot air layers bends until it reflects). Technological: optical fibre — light stays guided by repeated total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary, carrying data with almost no loss.

questions.question: A swimming pool always appears shallower than it really is. Explain the path of the light that makes this happen.
questions.solution: Light from the pool floor travels from water (denser) to air (rarer) and bends AWAY from the normal. The eye traces the ray backward in a straight line and therefore places the image closer to the surface than the true object — apparent depth = real depth / μ. The pool is not shallow; refraction mislocates the bottom.

questions.concept: Total internal reflection needs two conditions
questions.question: Light at 45° in glass (μ = 1.5) totally internally reflects, but 45° in water (μ = 1.33) does not. Why?
questions.solution: TIR needs BOTH denser-to-rarer travel AND an angle beyond the critical angle sin C = 1/μ. For glass C = 41.8°, so 45° exceeds it and TIR occurs; for water C = 48.8°, so 45° is still inside it and light refracts out. Both conditions must hold — satisfying one alone is not enough.

questions.concept: Why a fish sees a compressed world
questions.question: A fish looking up sees the entire sky squeezed into a cone of about 97°. Why is there a bright circle above it?
questions.solution: The critical angle for water is ~48.8°, so all directions in the outside world arrive within a 48.8° half-angle cone — the whole sky compressed into it. Beyond that angle, the fish sees total internal reflection of the water's own depths instead of sky, making a darker surrounding region and a bright circular 'window' overhead.
